extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalism students, scholars, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the role, operacionalization, indicators, predictors, and practices of watchdog (investigative) journalism — how watchdog reporting is conducted and what makes it effective or identifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog journalism role / purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Watchdog journalism is a form of investigative journalism in which journalists, authors or publishers of a news publication fact-check and interview political and public figures to increase accountability in democratic governance systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watchdog journalists gather information about the actions of people in power and inform the public in order to hold elected officials to account; they play a role as the fourth estate and publicize scandals, corruption, and failures to address public needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional distance / independence
rubrics_metrics.description: This requires maintaining a certain professional distance from people in power; watchdog journalists are different from propagandist journalists in that they report from an independent, nongovernmental perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain journalistic autonomy and independence from government and vested interests so reporting can critically scrutinize those in power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity of scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three operationalization dimensions: watchdog journalism has a few levels of scrutiny in terms of its reporting style (questions/interrogations; denunciation; strategies to elicit confession).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowest level: questions and interrogations. Next level: denunciation with more obvious and somewhat aggressive questions. Highest level: strategies designed for investigated persons to confess wrongdoing, which requires using a variety of evidence of wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three operationalization dimensions: the voice used to address scrutiny — journalists' own voice or a third party's voice are the most general types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a detached orientation, it is likely to use a third party's voice to question, criticize, and denounce wrongdoings rather than using the journalist's own voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of news event
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three operationalization dimensions: the type of event that watchdog journalism is interested in (e.g., corruption, judiciary processes, external investigations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detached orientations often handle issues about judiciary processes or external investigations and corruption in relationships between people with power and media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy and press freedom as predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Watchdog journalism can work effectively in well-established democratic countries, owing to the high level of the freedom of the press, journalistic autonomy and independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low levels of press censorship, state intervention, and institutional control are conducive to watchdog performance; strong democratic institutions predict more effective watchdog reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience orientation as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience orientation of a media outlet affects the performance of watchdog roles (e.g., market newspapers vs official newspapers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market or popular newspapers are more likely to play a watchdog role than official newspapers; differences in reporting style appear between popular and elite press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media political leaning as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: The political orientation of the journalism is closely associated with the performance of the watchdog role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media that serve interests of the right or moderates are less likely to work as watchdogs than media serving interests of the left; partisan bias affects coverage of political issues or scandals.

rubrics_metrics.name: News beats / specialization as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic specialization influences watchdog performance: journalists who deal with political issues are highly likely to act as watchdogs compared to those who cover business issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watchdog journalism is more prevalent on political beats; business/economy journalists are less likely to play the watchdog role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detached watchdog characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Detached watchdog journalism emphasizes neutrality, fairness, objectivity, and impartiality and refers to observing issues in a detached manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detached watchdogs tend to play a passive role in investigating people in power, relying more on third-party sources and external prompts rather than interventionist approaches; this form is predominant in many Western countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questioning by sources (indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: People other than journalists can question people in power by expressing opinions and giving statements or quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of sourced questioning indicates a detached orientation where sources prompt scrutiny rather than journalists directly leading it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism by sources (indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: People other than journalists can criticize those with power through expressing negative opinions or giving a statement or quote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sourced criticism appearing in coverage is an operational sign of detached watchdog reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denunciation by sources (indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: People other than journalists can provide a testimony or evidence about something that people with power do and say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sourced denunciations (testimonies, evidence) are used by detached watchdogs to publicize wrongdoing without the journalist adopting a direct accusatory voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: External investigation (indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corruption, scandals, or issues of people in power are often scrutinized and covered by the news media even though journalists do not handle them directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage that follows external probes, court cases, or investigations is a common mode of detached watchdog journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questioning by the journalist (indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can work as a watchdog by checking the legitimacy and integrity of people in power's actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct questioning by journalists signals an active watchdog function and can vary in intensity from routine checks to aggressive interrogation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism by the journalist (indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are allowed to judge and condemn what people in power do by making assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When journalists explicitly criticize actions of the powerful, coverage shifts from detached to more interventionist watchdog behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denunciation by the journalist (indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can denounce and accuse something that is hidden illegally by people in power by making assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic denunciation is a higher-intensity tactic that involves making affirmative accusations based on evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of conflict (indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can bring a source, an institution, or people in power that have to be scrutinized to the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate reporting that frames a conflict or contest around alleged wrongdoing is a way watchdog journalism prompts public accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anonymous sources and whistleblowers
rubrics_metrics.description: Watchdog investigations often rely on anonymous sources or whistleblowers as key material (e.g., Watergate's Deep Throat), plus in-depth interviews and documentary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret meetings, protected sources, interviews with insiders, documents, and recordings can be central to uncovering wrongdoing; such methods require careful source protection and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational resourcing and local news sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: The survival and health of local news organizations is critical to watchdog capacity; closures of local papers reduce watchdog coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decline in independent local newspapers harms the ability to investigate and expose corruption and leads to less transparency and accountability at local levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit expectation that stories demand official response
rubrics_metrics.description: Watchdog stories implicitly demand the response of public officials and can force governments to meet obligations by publicizing scandals and failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good watchdog reporting aims to produce public or institutional responses (e.g., investigations, resignations) and thus should present findings in ways that make follow-up action likely.
